title: India-Born Jazz Guitarist Pritesh Walia Detained by ICE Despite Artist Visa
excerpt: The New Delhi-born musician, a Berklee and New England Conservatory graduate who has performed and taught across the U.S., was detained by immigration authorities, adding to a growing list of Indian nationals caught up in enforcement actions.
body:
• Pritesh Walia, an India-born jazz guitarist with degrees from Berklee College of Music and New England Conservatory, has been detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement.
  • Walia held an Artist Visa but reportedly had his ability to work halted shortly after receiving it, leaving him in financial and legal limbo.
  • Fellow musicians have launched a recovery fundraiser for Walia, describing him as a selfless community member under immense stress.
  • His case adds to a growing pattern of Indian nationals — including students, professionals, and artists — facing ICE enforcement actions.

Pritesh Walia, an India-born jazz guitarist who spent over a decade building a career in the United States through elite music institutions and professional performance, has been detained by U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement, according to a report by NRI Pulse.

Walia, who hails from New Delhi, is a graduate of the Musicians Institute College of Contemporary Music in Los Angeles, Berklee College of Music in Boston, and the New England Conservatory, where he earned a master's degree in jazz performance. He has performed at venues across the U.S. and internationally, including multiple appearances at the Panama Jazz Festival.

A Career Built in America

Walia's musical journey began at age 13 with Indian classical music before he turned to jazz and moved to the United States for higher education. Over the years, he earned recognition including the Steve Vai Scholarship at Musicians Institute, the Berklee Achievement Scholarship, and the Dean Scholarship at New England Conservatory.

https://youtube.com/watch?v=9qrxAPdmBCc

Beyond performing, Walia established himself as a jazz educator, teaching at Bunker Hill Community College, Brookline Music School, and Excelsia College in Sydney. He held the guitar chair at the NEC Jazz Orchestra, performing alongside musicians such as Maria Schneider, and released his debut album "Hopetown" in 2024 to positive reviews.

He is endorsed by brands including Collings Guitars, Gruvgear, Chicken Picks, and Antelope Audio.

Work Halted After Visa Approval

According to a GoFundMe campaign launched by fellow musician Joey Rosin, Walia's ability to work was "abruptly halted just a month after receiving his Artist Visa," leaving him unable to support himself financially.

"Pritesh's natural inclination to give rather than receive has made it exceptionally difficult for him to ask for financial support. He is widely known as a selfless individual who is always there for others."

— Joey Rosin, musician and fundraiser organizer

The fundraiser describes Walia as experiencing "immense mental and financial stress" and is intended to provide stability while he navigates what is described as a difficult chapter in his life.

Part of a Broader Pattern

Walia's detention is the latest in a series of cases involving Indian nationals facing ICE enforcement actions across the United States. Under the current administration's aggressive immigration enforcement posture, Indian students, professionals, and artists have been among those detained, often in cases where visa status is disputed or administrative lapses are cited.

The United Nations human rights chief has raised concerns about conditions in ICE detention facilities, noting 18 deaths in ICE custody in the first five months of 2026 alone.

For the Indian-American arts community, Walia's case underscores the vulnerability of immigrant artists who contribute to American cultural life but often depend on temporary visa categories that offer limited protections.

What's Next

Details of the specific immigration charges or proceedings against Walia have not been publicly disclosed. The GoFundMe campaign continues to raise funds for his recovery and legal expenses. Fellow musicians and members of the jazz community have rallied around Walia, describing him as a vital contributor to the American jazz scene whose situation reflects broader systemic challenges facing immigrant artists.
nri_angle: Walia's detention highlights the precarious immigration status many Indian-born artists and professionals face in the U.S., even when they hold valid visas and have deep professional roots in the country.
